311.event_title: John Woolman refuses to write wills that bequeath enslaved people
311.event: As a young clerk in the early 1740s, the Quaker John Woolman was asked to write a bill of sale for an enslaved woman; he did so against his conscience but told his employer he believed slavery was inconsistent with Christianity. Afterwards, working as a tailor and scrivener who depended on the goodwill of his customers, he refused to draw up wills in which enslaved people would be passed on to heirs, telling one respected neighbour that he could not write his will without breaking his own peace. He went on to spend much of his life persuading Quakers to free those they held in slavery, and his Journal was published in 1775.
311.explanation: Woolman chose to lose business and risk offending respected customers rather than earn fees from documents that would keep human beings in bondage.
311.tie_back: The kural says the stainless hold firmly to the rule of never causing pain, even when harming others would bring wealth and standing, and Woolman turned away paid work rather than lend his pen to slavery.
311._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of refusing gain that depends on others' suffering, though the income Woolman gave up was modest rather than the great wealth the kural imagines; sources differ on his exact age in 1742.

312.event_title: Six-year-old Ruby Bridges prays for the crowds who jeered her
312.place: William Frantz Elementary School, New Orleans, Louisiana, United States
312.event: On 14 November 1960 six-year-old Ruby Bridges, escorted by federal marshals, became the only Black pupil at William Frantz Elementary School under a federal desegregation order. Crowds gathered daily to shout slurs and threats at her, and white parents withdrew their children, so she was taught alone by the one teacher who stayed. The child psychiatrist Robert Coles, who met her every week, reported that she told him she prayed for the people in the street, asking God to forgive them because they did not know what they were doing.
312.explanation: Faced with daily hostility she had done nothing to provoke, a small child answered with prayer for her tormentors rather than resentment.
312.tie_back: The kural says the stainless make it their rule not to hurt in return even those who have spitefully harmed them, and Ruby Bridges met spite with prayers for the very people who abused her.
312._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of returning no harm for spite; the account of her prayers comes from Robert Coles, who knew her at the time.

313.event_title: Henry II does public penance at Canterbury after Becket's murder
313.event: King Henry II and Archbishop Thomas Becket, once close friends, quarrelled bitterly for years over the rights of the Church, and Becket spent six years in exile. Soon after Becket's return, four of Henry's knights, reportedly acting on the king's angry words although there is no evidence he ordered it, killed the archbishop in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170. Becket was declared a saint in 1173, and in 1174 Henry walked barefoot through Canterbury, submitted to beatings by bishops and monks, and kept an overnight vigil at the shrine as penance.
313.explanation: The king's anger at an opponent who had defied him led to a crime that shocked Europe and left a stain on his reign that he could not escape.
313.tie_back: The kural warns that striking back with harm at those who opposed and hated you brings sorrow that cannot be escaped, and Henry's angry outburst against his adversary ended in public humiliation and lasting disgrace.
313._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Becket's opposition was a matter of principle rather than unprovoked hatred, and Henry's responsibility for the killing is disputed.

314.event_title: Gandhi gives Jan Smuts a pair of sandals he made himself
314.event: In South Africa Mohandas Gandhi led nonviolent campaigns against discriminatory laws enforced by General Jan Smuts and was imprisoned several times. Before leaving for India in 1914, after the two men reached an agreement, Gandhi sent Smuts a pair of leather sandals he had made with his own hands. In 1939, in a tribute written for Gandhi's 70th birthday, Smuts recalled that he had worn the sandals for many summers, though he felt he was not worthy to stand in the shoes of so great a man.
314.explanation: Gandhi answered his adversary not with bitterness but with a personal gift, and the gesture eventually drew from Smuts a public tribute of humility and respect.
314.tie_back: The kural says the true way to punish those who have harmed you is to do them such kindness that they feel ashamed, and Gandhi's handmade gift led his old opponent to declare himself unworthy to stand in his shoes.
314._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural; accounts differ on whether Smuts physically returned the sandals in 1939 or only wrote of them.

315.event_title: Joseph Rotblat leaves the Manhattan Project
315.place: Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States
315.event: The Polish-born physicist Joseph Rotblat worked on atomic bomb research at Liverpool and from 1944 at Los Alamos, having joined because he feared Nazi Germany might build such a weapon. In late 1944, when it became clear that Germany was not close to developing an atomic bomb, he left the Manhattan Project on grounds of conscience. He turned his research toward the medical uses of radiation, co-founded the Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs in 1957, and shared the 1995 Nobel Peace Prize with Pugwash for efforts to eliminate nuclear weapons.
315.explanation: Rotblat refused to let his scientific knowledge serve a weapon whose purpose he could no longer justify, and spent the rest of his life using science to reduce suffering.
315.tie_back: The kural asks what good knowledge is if one does not treat others' pain as one's own and guard them from it, and Rotblat chose to put his learning to protecting people rather than harming them.
315._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of knowledge placed under the rule of compassion; one source describes his departure as ostensibly on grounds of conscience.

316.event_title: Hiroshima unveils the Cenotaph and its vow never to repeat the evil
316.place: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park, Hiroshima, Japan
316.event: On 6 August 1952 the Cenotaph for the A-bomb Victims, designed by Kenzo Tange, was unveiled at Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Ceremony; its stone chest holds the register of those who died from the bombing, regardless of nationality. Its inscription was written by Tadayoshi Saika, a Hiroshima University professor and himself an A-bomb survivor, after Mayor Shinzo Hamai asked for words expressing both a prayer and a vow. The English reads: "Let all the souls here rest in peace; For we shall not repeat the evil." Saika intended the vow to be made by all human beings.
316.explanation: A city that had suffered the first atomic bombing chose to answer its own experience of pain with a vow that no one should inflict such suffering again.
316.tie_back: The kural says that whatever you have learned through your own experience to be painful, you must never do to another, and Hiroshima's survivors turned what they had suffered into a public vow never to repeat it.
316._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the negative golden rule drawn from lived suffering; the meaning of the word we in the inscription has been debated.

317.event_title: The Nuremberg Code sets limits on human experimentation
317.event: On 19 August 1947 the judges of the American military tribunal in the Doctors' Trial at Nuremberg, which tried German physicians for crimes committed in the concentration camps, delivered their verdict. In a section titled Permissible Medical Experiments they set out ten principles, later known as the Nuremberg Code. These require that the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential and that experiments be conducted so as to avoid all unnecessary physical and mental suffering and injury.
317.explanation: After revelations of terrible abuses, the Code became a landmark statement that medical research must not inflict needless suffering on any person.
317.tie_back: The kural calls it the highest virtue never to do any harm, however small, to anyone at any time, and the Nuremberg Code wrote a version of that principle into the foundations of modern medical ethics.
317._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the Code forbids unnecessary suffering and still permits some risk, whereas the kural demands total non-harm even in thought.

318.event_title: Anna Sewell writes Black Beauty to win kindness for horses
318.event: Anna Sewell, who was disabled from a young age and had difficulty walking, spent the last years of her life confined to her house as an invalid while writing Black Beauty, a fictional autobiography of a horse. She stated that one of her aims was to induce kindness, sympathy and an understanding treatment of horses. The book, first published in 1877 by Jarrold of Norwich, is said to have been instrumental in ending the cruel use of the checkrein, or bearing rein.
318.explanation: Sewell used her final years to make readers feel the suffering of animals from the inside, by telling the story in the horse's own voice.
318.tie_back: The kural asks why anyone who knows pain in his own life would inflict it on other living beings, and Sewell's book made readers recognise in a horse's suffering the same pain they knew themselves.
318._accuracy_note: Reasonable: the book appeals to shared capacity for pain across species, but the sources do not say that Sewell's own suffering was her stated motive.

319.event_title: Danton is tried and executed by the Revolutionary Tribunal he helped create
319.event: In March 1793 Georges Danton played an instrumental role in establishing the Revolutionary Tribunal, and the following month he helped create the Committee of Public Safety, laying groundwork for the Reign of Terror. When he later opposed the Terror, he was arrested on the night of 29-30 March 1794 and tried before that same Revolutionary Tribunal from 2 to 4 April. He was executed by guillotine in Paris on 5 April 1794.
319.explanation: Within about a year, the instrument of harm that Danton had helped build was turned against him.
319.tie_back: The kural warns that if you harm others in the morning, harm will come back to you by the afternoon, and Danton was condemned by the very tribunal he had helped set up barely a year earlier.
319._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of harm swiftly rebounding on its author, though Danton's downfall came from opposing the Terror rather than as direct punishment for creating the Tribunal.

320.event_title: Vidkun Quisling's collaboration ends in his trial and execution
320.event: During the German invasion of Norway in April 1940, Vidkun Quisling proclaimed himself head of a new government, and from 1942 he served as Minister President of a Nazi-controlled puppet government. He signed laws that enabled the arrest of Norway's Jewish men and the confiscation of Jewish property, and 772 Norwegian Jews were deported, most to their deaths at Auschwitz. After Norway's liberation in May 1945 he was arrested, convicted of treason and other crimes, and executed at Akershus Fortress in Oslo on 24 October 1945; his name became a synonym for traitor.
320.explanation: The man who helped bring great suffering on his own country ended his life condemned by it, his very name turned into a word of disgrace.
320.tie_back: The kural says all suffering falls upon those who cause suffering, and Quisling's betrayal of his people returned on him as condemnation and a lasting byword for treachery.
320._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the outcome came through a court's judgment rather than as a natural consequence of the harm itself, and the kural's second line about avoiding harm to stay free of suffering is only implied.
